question_text: For a continuous function $f(x)$ defined on the interval $a \leqslant x \leqslant b$, the length of the curve can be found using $L = \int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1+[f'(x)]^2}\,dx$. Find the length of:

mark_breakdown.desc: Evaluating arc length numerically to 3 significant figures: $1.48$

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Arc length of a curve given by $y = f(x)$ is $L = \int_a^b \sqrt{1 + [f'(x)]^2}\,dx$.
step_by_step: Substitute into the arc length formula: $L = \int_0^1 \sqrt{1 + 4x^2}\,dx$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Forgetting to square the derivative inside the square root.

mark_breakdown.desc: Setting up arc length integral $L = \int_0^\pi \sqrt{1 + \cos^2 x}\,dx$
Evaluating arc length numerically to 3 significant figures: $3.82$

subparts.solution: $f(x) = \sin x, \ 0 \le x \le \pi \implies f'(x) = \cos x$. So, $L = \int_0^{\pi} \sqrt{1 + \cos^2 x}\,dx \approx 3.82\text{ units}$

step_by_step: Evaluate the integral numerically using GDC in radian mode.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Confusing the derivative of $\sin x$ as $-\cos x$ (though squared it gives the same, good practice is essential).
